hero.title: Types of Majorities
hero.description: Master the constitutional classifications of majorities in the Indian Parliament: Simple, Absolute, Effective, and the four types of Special Majorities, with their applications and requirements.

timeline.title: Evolution of Majorities in the Parliament
timeline.description: Trace the historic milestones and amendments that shaped majority requirements in the Indian Constitution.

cards.details: The Constitution of India comes into force, establishing the original majority frameworks under Article 61 (Presidential Impeachment), Article 249 (State List legislation), Article 312 (All India Services), and Article 368 (Amendment).
The first constitutional amendment was passed, validating the use of the Special Majority Type 3 (Article 368 + State Ratification) for land reforms and creation of the Ninth Schedule.

The Supreme Court ruled that while Parliament can amend the Constitution using Article 368 Special Majority, it cannot alter the Basic Structure, placing judicial checks on the majoritarian legislative power.

In response to the Emergency abuses, the Janata Party government amended Article 352, upgrading the majority required to approve a National Emergency from a simple majority to a Special Majority (Type 2).

mnemonics.title: Mnemonics & Memory Hacks
mnemonics.description: Use these visual memory hooks to retain critical facts about the Types of Majorities for the UPSC Civil Services Examination.

items.title: Mnemonic 1: Base Majorities
items.decryption: Remember the three basic majorities: **S**imple (Present & voting), **A**bsolute (Total strength), and **E**ffective (Total minus vacancies).

items.title: Mnemonic 2: Special Majority Types
items.decryption: Remember the four special types: **Type 1** (2/3 Present & Voting), **Type 2** (2/3 P&V + 50% Total), **Type 3** (Type 2 + 50% State Assemblies), and **Type 4** (2/3 of Total strength).

flashcards.title: Active Recall Flashcards
flashcards.description: Use these active recall questions to reinforce fact-dense syllabus details on parliamentary majorities.

items.question: What is the difference between Absolute and Effective strength of a House?
items.answer: Absolute strength is the total sanctioned seats in the House (e.g., 543 in Lok Sabha). Effective strength is the total sanctioned seats minus any vacant seats caused by death, resignation, or disqualification.

items.question: Which majority is required for the removal of the Vice President of India?
items.answer: An Effective Majority in the Rajya Sabha (acting as a resolution for removal) and a Simple Majority (agreement) in the Lok Sabha.

items.question: What majority is required to pass a Constitutional Amendment Bill under Article 368?
items.answer: A Special Majority Type 2: A majority of not less than 2/3 of the members present and voting in each House, which must also be supported by more than 50% of the total strength of that House.

items.question: Which constitutional amendments are passed by a Simple Majority?
items.answer: Amendments relating to the admission/establishment of new states, changing state boundaries/names (Articles 2, 3, 4), and abolition or creation of Legislative Councils in states (Article 169) are passed by a Simple Majority and are not deemed to be amendments under Article 368.

items.question: What majority is required for the impeachment of the President of India under Article 61?
items.answer: A Special Majority Type 4: A majority of not less than 2/3 of the total strength of the House. This is the most stringent majority required under the Indian Constitution.

traps.title: UPSC Prelims Traps to Avoid
items: Trap 1: Do not confuse effective majority with absolute majority. Effective majority excludes vacant seats, while absolute majority considers the total sanctioned strength. In a house with many vacancies, the effective majority threshold is lower than absolute.

Trap 2: Watch out for options claiming that all constitutional amendments require a Special Majority. Certain amendments like creation/abolition of legislative councils (Article 169) or altering state areas/boundaries (Article 3) only require a simple majority and are explicitly excluded from Article 368.

Trap 3: The impeachment of the President (Article 61) requires a majority of 2/3 of the total strength of the House, NOT 2/3 of present and voting. A common trap is to treat it like other special majorities.

Trap 4: For the removal of the Vice President, Rajya Sabha must pass the resolution by an effective majority, but Lok Sabha only needs to agree to it by a simple majority. Options claiming a special majority or effective majority in both houses are incorrect.

deepDive.title: Syllabus Core Study Notes (Deep-Dive)
deepDive.description: Master the definition, mathematical models, constitutional articles, and real-world applications of all majorities in the Indian Parliament.

sections.title: 1. Simple, Absolute, and Effective Majorities
sections.content:
Majorities under the Indian Constitution are classified based on the baseline headcount required to pass a bill or resolution. Understanding the distinct mathematical formulations and exclusions is essential for UPSC Prelims.

Simple Majority

Also known as **Ordinary Majority**. It requires more than 50% of the members **present and voting** in the House.

  • Formula: > 50% of (Members Present - Members Abstaining).
  • Primary Use: Passing ordinary, financial, or money bills; passing no-confidence, confidence, or adjournment motions; declaring President's rule (Article 356) or financial emergency (Article 360).
  • Example: In Lok Sabha (543 seats), if 300 are present and 50 abstain, simple majority is > 50% of 250 = 126 votes.
Effective Majority

Requires more than 50% of the **effective strength** of the House, which is total sanctioned strength minus vacant seats.

  • Formula: > 50% of (Total Strength - Vacancies).
  • Primary Use: Removal of the Vice President of India in Rajya Sabha (Article 67(b)); removal of Speaker and Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha/State Assemblies.
  • Example: If Lok Sabha total strength is 543 and 13 seats are vacant, effective strength is 530. Effective majority requires > 50% of 530 = 266 votes.

Absolute Majority

An **Absolute Majority** requires more than 50% of the **total sanctioned strength** of the House, regardless of vacancies or absent members. Formula: > 50% of Total Seats. For instance, in Lok Sabha, this is always 272 votes (50% of 543 + 1). While no bill is passed using an absolute majority alone, it forms the threshold for government formation and is integrated as a checking clause in Special Majorities (Article 368).

sections.title: 2. Special Majorities (Types 1, 2, 3, and 4)
sections.content:
Special majorities are used for sensitive matters such as constitutional amendments, impeachment of key heads of state, or overriding federal divisions. The Indian Constitution specifies four distinct types of Special Majorities.

Type 1 (Articles 249 & 312)

Requires **not less than 2/3 of members present and voting**.

  • Use: Authorizing Parliament to legislate on State List (Article 249) or creating a new All-India Service (Article 312) in Rajya Sabha.
Type 2 (Article 368)

Requires a **dual condition**: 2/3 of present and voting AND more than 50% of total strength of the house.

  • Use: Constitutional Amendment Bills; removal of Supreme Court/High Court Judges, CAG, CEC; approval/extension of National Emergency (Article 352).
Type 3 (Article 368 + Federal Ratification)

Requires the **Article 368 Special Majority** in Parliament plus **ratification by simple majority from more than half of the State Legislatures**.

  • Use: Amending federal provisions (e.g., electing the President, representation of states in Parliament, distribution of legislative powers between center and states).
Type 4 (Article 61)

Requires **not less than 2/3 of the total strength** of the House. This is the strictest majority.

  • Use: Impeachment of the President of India. In Lok Sabha, this requires at least 362 votes, regardless of present members or vacancies.

Summary Table of Majorities

Type Mathematical Requirement Constitutional Article / Purpose
Simple > 50% of present & voting Ordinary bills, Money bills, No-Confidence motion
Effective > 50% of effective strength (total - vacancies) Removal of Vice President (Rajya Sabha), Speaker (Lok Sabha)
Absolute > 50% of total strength of House Government formation (threshold benchmark)
Special (Type 1) >= 2/3 of present & voting Articles 249 and 312 (Rajya Sabha resolution)
Special (Type 2) >= 2/3 of P&V AND > 50% of total strength Article 368 (Constitutional Amendment), SC/HC judge removal
Special (Type 3) Special (Type 2) + simple majority from > 50% states Article 368 (Federal provisions amendment)
Special (Type 4) >= 2/3 of total strength of House Article 61 (Impeachment of President)
